doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Great Lakes happy hours: Lunceford, Eddie Peabody, raiding the band
summary: Entertainment at Great Lakes includes the Lunceford band; the Chief gets the band out before it is raided and returns to California.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: turn, do your about face and we had one guy, a real tall handsome guy, they made him the band leader.
Yeah. With the baton kind of?
Yeah. And so they would have happy hours. And when they would have happy hours you would have the entertainment that would come in. One happy hour they had the Jimmy Lunceford Orchestra.

Oh man. And they were hot then. You know, 1942, they were hot. They had all these wonderful arrangements and they were a first class band. Willie Smith was in that band, along with Gerald Wilson and —

Snooky was in it, yeah. Joe Thomas. Oh and Jessie Crawford the drummer, outstanding. So that was one time. And so the Commander, the fellow who was in charge of the music program, was Eddie Peabody, the banjo player. And he would, during the happy hours, he would always perform. And he was outstanding. And then of course one of the requirements for being released from training was you had to parade in front of him and do your maneuvers and everything. But he was a great guy you know. Because he was a performer. He wasn’t strictly Navy. He had been in World War I and so he was in the Reserves, so through the Reserves he just kept increasing his rank. So he was a Commander. And so anyhow what happened, our Chief, he was trying to get us out of there as soon as possible because the Chief from the ship’s company band at Great Lakes, he was trying to raid the band. Because he had Ernie Royal, who was on the “Flying Home” high notes — Ernie was noted for high notes plus he was a fine player. Of course Marshall — because the fellas would have jam sessions. And the other Chief would be there watching to see who could do what. So they were trying to raid our band. So our Chief, he was old Navy. He had an armful of gold stripes you know, indicating like the service gold, so that meant that he was 1A, you know, never had any disciplinary problems or anything. So anyhow he got us out of there and then we came back to California. And on December 1st — because we spent Thanksgiving there at Great Lakes. We had a turkey dinner. And then of course on the train coming back there was no jam session. Because we were Navy then, oh yes. So anyhow we came back and we went there to St. Mary’s and then we were lucky because see besides being stationed there you lived off the base. So that’s one of the reasons I guess they recruited us from this area. So we were given quarters and subsistence, besides our Navy pay — what was it $66 a month — and they took out $12 for family allowance if you were married.
